intro: Hebrew Bible, Apocrypha and New Testament, read in the New Oxford Annotated Bible (NRSV). Reading approach: literary, historical and theological analysis, not historical verification. Update this file as the reading continues.

conclusions.title: The Bible is a Rorschach test.
conclusions.body: Largely supported. The same texts were used to defend and attack slavery, to demand and to forbid political obedience (Romans 13 versus Revelation 13), to support and to oppose women's ordination, and to justify opposite views on predestination, the millennium and images. The text underdetermines doctrine. It isn't "anything goes," though. Some readings need much more interpretive strain than others, and the historical-critical method exists to tell them apart.

conclusions.title: No coherent narrative or ethics; even 'thou shalt not kill' is malleable.
conclusions.body: Half right. The ethics are inconsistent, and the clearest cases are the ones you identified: violence against outsiders is celebrated, while violence against insiders is punished; slavery is accepted; women are subordinated; God commands what other texts forbid. On the commandment itself, the Hebrew verb (*ratsach*) usually means unlawful killing or murder, so the real conflict is less "thou shalt not kill" versus war than *who counts* as protected. That is your in-group/out-group point. A narrative does run through the canon (covenant, kingship, exile and return, hope for restoration), but it was imposed by editors and later readers, not by one author.

conclusions.title: A series of books over a thousand years, each with its own agenda.
conclusions.body: The strongest of the three, and mainstream scholarly consensus. Most contradictions you found (Samuel/Chronicles, Matthew/Luke genealogies, Matthew/Acts on Judas, Job's frame versus its speeches) are what a composite library produces. Believers who read it as one book have to harmonize, and the harmonizations were often the weakest part of what we discussed.

themes.trajectory: None (Pentateuch) → shadowy Sheol (Psalms, Job) → total cessation (Ecclesiastes) → hints (Isaiah 24-27, Psalm 49) → resurrection (Daniel 12, 2 Maccabees 7) → heaven and hell (2 Esdras) → eternal torment and immortality (Revelation)
Other gods exist (Exodus, "God of gods," "jealous") → Deuteronomy transitional → explicit denial (Second Isaiah) → Paul still says "many gods" (1 Cor 8:5)
Talking serpent → "the satan" as role in Job → "Satan" inciting David (Chronicles) → named demons (Tobit) → cosmic enemy (NT) → identified with the serpent (Revelation 12:9)
"Anointed" = kings and priests → hope for restored David line → Elijah/messenger (Malachi) → "my son the Messiah" (2 Esdras) → Jesus
Empowered human agent (Acts 10:38) → pre-existent Word (John) → Hebrews 1 and Revelation's shared titles → Nicaea. Arian and Trinitarian readings both cite the same verses
God's breath/power → "his holy spirit" → personal Paraclete (John) → Trinity (4th century)
Anger/compassion oscillation, changeable God, God hardening hearts, God "setting people up" (Eden to the beast of Revelation 13)
Celebrated against outsiders (herem, Maccabees); non-retaliation taught in the NT but retribution deferred to Christ as judge
Purity laws, silence texts, household codes, "equality after death, hierarchy in life"
Matthew 24:34, 1 Corinthians 7, 2 Peter's reply to the delay

notes.heading: Genesis
notes.note: The serpent of Genesis 3 is never called Satan; that identification is later (Revelation 12:9).

notes.heading: Genesis
notes.note: Abraham marries his half-sister (20:12), later forbidden in Leviticus.

notes.heading: Genesis
notes.note: Table of Nations (ch. 10) and Babel explain the world's peoples without separate creator gods.

notes.heading: Genesis
notes.note: Circumcision (ch. 17) is given as a covenant sign with no stated rationale; it works as an identity marker.

notes.heading: Genesis
notes.note: Polygamy among the patriarchs goes uncondemned.

notes.heading: Exodus
notes.note: "Who is like you among the gods?" and "no other gods before me" assume other gods exist.

notes.heading: Exodus
notes.note: God relents after the golden calf when Moses argues.

notes.heading: Exodus
notes.note: Jealousy implies rivals.

notes.heading: Leviticus
notes.note: Sibling relations are prohibited (18, 20), but Abraham and Jacob's marriages (sisters) show the later date of the law.

notes.heading: Leviticus
notes.note: Menstruation and childbirth cause ritual impurity. *Observation: the contradiction between God designing female biology and that biology being impure is never addressed anywhere in the Bible.*

notes.heading: Leviticus
notes.note: Sukkot/booths, consecration of houses and animals (ch. 27), the Jubilee (never practiced).

notes.heading: Leviticus
notes.note: Orthodox Judaism still keeps Sukkot, but there is no Temple, so no sacrifice or consecration system.

notes.heading: Numbers
notes.note: Bitter-water ordeal (ch. 5): magical, not toxicological, and applied only to wives.

notes.heading: Numbers
notes.note: Anakim giants: narrative function, not history.

notes.heading: Numbers
notes.note: "Wilderness" as testing ground. A population of 600,000 men is archaeologically absent.

notes.heading: Numbers
notes.note: Bronze serpent (ch. 21), later destroyed as Nehushtan.

notes.heading: Deuteronomy
notes.note: All rewards and punishments are earthly and generational; no afterlife.

notes.heading: Deuteronomy
notes.note: Centralization of worship explains the later condemnation of "high places."

notes.heading: Deuteronomy
notes.note: Intermarriage ban targets the seven Canaanite nations on religious grounds.

notes.heading: Deuteronomy
notes.note: Non-sacrificial slaughter permitted (ch. 12), not a contradiction of Leviticus.

notes.heading: Deuteronomy
notes.note: Polygamy accepted; polyandry never.

notes.heading: Deuteronomy
notes.note: "God of gods" (10:17) is supremacy language, not exclusive monotheism.

notes.heading: Joshua and Judges
notes.note: The Caleb/Achsah story appears in both (a doublet).

notes.heading: Joshua and Judges
notes.note: Herem (total destruction) is presented as obedience.

notes.heading: Joshua and Judges
notes.note: Gideon's blood vengeance for two brothers versus thousands killed in war: no reflection on the double standard.

notes.heading: Joshua and Judges
notes.note: Abimelech's murder of 70 brothers on one stone is likely stylized.

notes.heading: Joshua and Judges
notes.note: Samson is a failed hero; the story resists a coherent moral.

notes.heading: 1-2 Samuel
notes.note: Anti-monarchical (1 Sam 8) and pro-monarchical (2 Sam 7) strands side by side.

notes.heading: 1-2 Samuel
notes.note: David executes the Amalekite messenger without verification. We already know from 1 Sam 31 that Saul killed himself, so the "he was lying" defense doesn't rescue David's justice.

notes.heading: 1-2 Samuel
notes.note: Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Sam 11): the text condemns it, but Bathsheba's agency is invisible.

notes.heading: 1-2 Samuel
notes.note: David's victory hymn (2 Sam 22 = Psalm 18) claims blamelessness after those events.

notes.heading: 1-2 Samuel
notes.note: The census: God incites it here, Satan in Chronicles.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Stock curse formula ("dogs shall eat...") against condemned dynasties, likely written after the fact.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Casualty numbers (100,000 killed in a day) are hyperbole.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Baal-zebub (a mocked Philistine god) becomes the NT's Beelzebul.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: High places were normal YHWH worship sites until the Deuteronomistic reforms.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Nehushtan: Moses's bronze serpent destroyed by Hezekiah.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Male cult prostitutes in the Temple (Josiah's reforms) show how mainstream syncretism was.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Annals formula ("are they not written in the Book of the Annals...?") is a citation convention.

notes.heading: 1-2 Kings
notes.note: Solomon's foreign wives are central to his fall here but absent from Chronicles.

notes.heading: 1-2 Chronicles
notes.note: Satan first appears as a named instigator (1 Chron 21:1), replacing God from 2 Sam 24:1.

notes.heading: 1-2 Chronicles
notes.note: Idealizes David and Solomon: omits Bathsheba, the foreign wives and apostasy.

notes.heading: 1-2 Chronicles
notes.note: Why counting people is a sin is never explained; pride and conscription are the leading theories.

notes.heading: Ezra-Nehemiah
notes.note: Forced divorce of foreign wives is much harsher than Deuteronomy.

notes.heading: Ezra-Nehemiah
notes.note: "Jews" as a term arises after the exile because only Judah survived.

notes.heading: Ezra-Nehemiah
notes.note: Language loss in mixed families is treated as an identity threat.

notes.heading: Job
notes.note: The frame story (a wager with "the satan") is incompatible with God's speeches about cosmic mystery.

notes.heading: Job
notes.note: Leviathan is a mythological chaos monster, not a whale; in Canaanite myth the storm god defeats it, in Job God created and controls it.

notes.heading: Job
notes.note: God vindicates Job's protest over the friends' defense of divine justice.

notes.heading: Psalms
notes.note: Sheol is passive silence: "in Sheol who can give you praise?"

notes.heading: Psalms
notes.note: "Brought up from Sheol" (Ps 30) is rescue language; the text is ambiguous enough that it can be read more literally.

notes.heading: Psalms
notes.note: Psalm 49 is ambiguous on afterlife; Psalm 51:5 is not original sin.

notes.heading: Psalms
notes.note: Sacrifice is downplayed in favor of a contrite heart, which later enabled worship without the Temple.

notes.heading: Psalms
notes.note: Psalm 117 is universal praise, not evangelism; "awake my soul" (Ps 57:8, 108:2), not Proverbs, is the Mumford & Sons phrase.

notes.heading: Proverbs
notes.note: The "cistern" passage (ch. 5) is about marital fidelity.

notes.heading: Proverbs
notes.note: Numerical sayings ("three things... four") are a poetic device, not counting.

notes.heading: Ecclesiastes
notes.note: "Nothing new under the sun" is from 1:9.

notes.heading: Ecclesiastes
notes.note: "The dead know nothing" (9:5-6) is the clearest statement of finality in the Bible.

notes.heading: Ecclesiastes
notes.note: 7:28 ("one man among a thousand... a woman not found") is plain misogyny.

notes.heading: Ecclesiastes
notes.note: The silver cord (12:6) is physical death imagery; "a time for everything" became "Turn! Turn! Turn!"

notes.heading: Ecclesiastes
notes.note: You found it the most sincere book; it was nearly excluded from the canon.

notes.heading: Song of Songs
notes.note: No mention of God; "my sister, my bride" is love-poetry convention, not incest.

notes.heading: Song of Songs
notes.note: Included via Solomonic attribution and allegory.

notes.heading: Song of Songs
notes.note: Catholic tradition allegorized away the eroticism, which conflicts with its shame-based sexual ethics.

notes.heading: Isaiah
notes.note: Second Isaiah gives the first explicit monotheism.

notes.heading: Isaiah
notes.note: Isaiah 24-27 has the first hints of resurrection ("your dead shall live").

notes.heading: Isaiah
notes.note: Chapter 23 is an oracle against Tyre.

notes.heading: Ezekiel
notes.note: God negotiates the dung used for baking bread (4:12-15).

notes.heading: Ezekiel
notes.note: Menstruation violations listed among Jerusalem's sins (22:10); Oholah and Oholibah are allegories for Samaria and Jerusalem.

notes.heading: Ezekiel
notes.note: Water from the Temple (ch. 47) is restoration imagery echoed in Revelation 22.

notes.heading: Ezekiel
notes.note: Ezekiel 18 rejects inherited guilt.

notes.heading: Daniel
notes.note: First explicit resurrection with differentiated fates (12:2).

notes.heading: Daniel
notes.note: "Prince of princes" in 8:25 means God, not a Messiah; I was wrong to suggest otherwise.

notes.heading: Daniel
notes.note: Post-facto prophecy of Antiochus IV; "Son of Man" appears in ch. 7.

notes.heading: Hosea
notes.note: "On the third day he will raise us up" (6:2) refers to national restoration. It may have supplied the "third day" motif for the resurrection narratives; that is plausible but unproven.

notes.heading: Zephaniah and the prophets on Moab
notes.note: Moab is consistently negative in the text. Moab, Utah (named 1855) probably took the name from landscape or biblical familiarity, not endorsement.

notes.heading: Malachi
notes.note: The nearest OT approach to hell ("burning like an oven") and to a messianic messenger (Elijah returning).

notes.heading: Tobit
notes.note: Named angel (Raphael) and named demon (Asmodeus), magic, Hades; a folktale genre unlike the canonical OT.

notes.heading: Tobit
notes.note: The sparrow-dropping blindness is medically plausible.

notes.heading: Sirach
notes.note: "Neither seek what is too difficult for you" (3:21) is conservative anti-speculation advice. Sirach 31 has the closest thing to table-manners rules, relevant to the "elbows" question; no Bible verse says it.

notes.heading: Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah
notes.note: "Everlasting joy" is national restoration, not afterlife.

notes.heading: Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah
notes.note: The anti-idol polemic uses menstrual impurity as a measure of worthlessness.

notes.heading: 1 Maccabees
notes.note: War elephants with towers are a likely source for Tolkien's oliphaunts. Revenge on a wedding party (9:37-41) is narrated approvingly.

notes.heading: 1 Maccabees
notes.note: "Gentile" comes from Latin *gentilis*, translating *goyim*/*ethne*.

notes.heading: 2 Maccabees
notes.note: Chapter 7 is the first explicit resurrection theology, driven by martyrdom (the old reward theology had failed).

notes.heading: 4 Maccabees
notes.note: "Reason" means Stoic self-mastery within Torah, not modern empirical reason.

notes.heading: 2 Esdras
notes.note: Written around 100 CE as pseudonymous prophecy. "My son the Messiah" dies after a 400-year reign.

notes.heading: 2 Esdras
notes.note: First clear heaven/hell dualism (7:36), with Persian influence.

notes.heading: 2 Esdras
notes.note: "Holy spirit" is more personal here, but not yet a distinct person.

notes.heading: Matthew
notes.note: The genealogy runs through Joseph while the virgin birth removes him.

notes.heading: Matthew
notes.note: Sermon on the Mount intensifies the law (thought crime, divorce); NT "relaxation" is Paul, not Jesus.

notes.heading: Matthew
notes.note: "Let the dead bury their dead," "call no one father," the failed "this generation" prophecy (24:34).

notes.heading: Matthew
notes.note: "Son of Man" is a multilayered title; in the parable of the weeds it clearly means Jesus.

notes.heading: Matthew
notes.note: Slavery is accepted; tax collectors were hated as Roman collaborators; baptism has no OT equivalent.

notes.heading: Mark
notes.note: No birth narrative; named brothers and sisters of Jesus (6:3), which is hard to square with perpetual virginity.

notes.heading: Mark
notes.note: Jesus's family thought he was out of his mind (3:21).

notes.heading: Mark
notes.note: "All foods clean" (7:19) is Mark's editorial gloss, which Matthew omits.

notes.heading: Mark
notes.note: The messianic secret goes wrong comically (can't stay hidden); demon dialogue (Legion) supports a literal reading, which is why only the literalist position is textually consistent.

notes.heading: Mark
notes.note: "Receive the kingdom as a child" is about manner, not age; marriage ends in the resurrection (12:25).

notes.heading: Luke and John
notes.note: Passion narratives never mention nails at the crucifixion; only John 20:25 mentions them, afterward.

notes.heading: Luke and John
notes.note: Luke 23:34 ("forgive them") is textually uncertain; Stephen's version in Acts 7 may have come first.

notes.heading: Luke and John
notes.note: John 17: the prayer of a Son who is "God" to the Father raises the Trinity problem.

notes.heading: Luke and John
notes.note: John increasingly blames "the Jews," a trajectory that fed centuries of antisemitism.

notes.heading: Acts
notes.note: Judas dies by hanging (Matthew) or by rupture (Acts 1); the field-purchase stories conflict.

notes.heading: Acts
notes.note: Peter's argument for Davidic descent depends on lineage the virgin birth undermines.

notes.heading: Acts
notes.note: "Hanging on a tree" means the cross (Deut 21:23).

notes.heading: Acts
notes.note: Acts 10:38 is "low" Christology; the Peter vision reverses dietary law.

notes.heading: Acts
notes.note: The "we" passages (16:10 onward) are debated: eyewitness, source, or convention.

notes.heading: Acts
notes.note: Acts 17:29 critiques images, which sits uneasily with church iconography.

notes.heading: Romans
notes.note: Universal "hearing" (10:18) conflicts with geography; God hardening hearts (11:8) is the recurring setup problem.

notes.heading: Romans
notes.note: Gentile inclusion is framed as making Israel jealous (11:11-14).

notes.heading: Romans
notes.note: Romans 12 ("do not repay evil") versus an eye for an eye; Romans 13 ("authorities are God's servants") reverses the Gospel tone.

notes.heading: Romans
notes.note: Romans 15:9-12 quotes genuine OT passages (Ps 18:49, Deut 32:43, Ps 117:1, Isa 11:10), but Paul builds more from them than they say.

notes.heading: Romans
notes.note: Tertius (16:22) was the scribe.

notes.heading: 1-2 Corinthians
notes.note: "God's foolishness" (1:25) is deliberate paradox.

notes.heading: 1-2 Corinthians
notes.note: 1 Cor 7: Paul expects the end soon; 8:5-6 states "many gods and many lords"; 14:34-35 (women silent) is probably an interpolation; chapter 13 is about church gifts, not weddings.

notes.heading: 1-2 Corinthians
notes.note: 2 Corinthians is partly a fundraising letter (ch. 8-9) and partly Paul's defense against unnamed "super-apostles."

notes.heading: Galatians
notes.note: Paul's law-versus-faith contrast fails the logic test you raised: both are claimed revelation, and Christianity's "believe or be lost" is as binary.

notes.heading: Galatians
notes.note: Circumcision is called both fatal and meaningless (5:2-6).

notes.heading: Galatians
notes.note: "Apostle" means "sent one"; Paul claims the title via vision, not acquaintance with Jesus.

notes.heading: Colossians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, Titus
notes.note: Household codes replicate Greco-Roman hierarchy: "equality after death, hierarchy during life."

notes.heading: Colossians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, Titus
notes.note: 1 Tim 1:10 condemns slave traders, i.e. kidnappers, not slavery. 1 Tim 2:9-15 bars women from teaching.

notes.heading: Colossians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, Titus
notes.note: The "bishop married once" line (1 Tim 3) and Catholic celibacy; "love of money" is the misquoted "root of evil."

notes.heading: Colossians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, Titus
notes.note: Titus 1:12 endorses a stereotype of Cretans while chapter 3 says speak evil of no one.

notes.heading: Hebrews
notes.note: Not Paul's. The "40 years" is the wilderness generation.

notes.heading: Hebrews
notes.note: Melchizedek priesthood sets aside descent, but Hebrews itself says Jesus came from Judah, so the factual contradiction is between Matthew and Luke, not Hebrews.

notes.heading: Hebrews
notes.note: "If the first covenant had been faultless" (8:7) concedes a flawed first covenant; Hebrews 1 reads comfortably in Arian terms.

notes.heading: Hebrews
notes.note: The OT never reveals a Trinity, which believers explain as progressive revelation.

notes.heading: James, 1-2 Peter, 1 John
notes.note: James: Jesus's brother named matter-of-factly; Catholic reading treats "brother" as kinsman. "Friendship with the world" means the status-driven social order.

notes.heading: James, 1-2 Peter, 1 John
notes.note: 1 Peter 2:23 "did not threaten" versus Jesus as final judge; the church's ostentation against "God opposes the proud."

notes.heading: James, 1-2 Peter, 1 John
notes.note: 2 Peter likely dates around 90-150 CE and answers the delay of the Second Coming.

notes.heading: James, 1-2 Peter, 1 John
notes.note: 1 John: sinlessness (3:6) versus "if we say we have no sin" (1:8); circular test of truth (4:6); a "mortal sin" (5:16-17) that Catholic theology later built on.

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: Author is probably not the apostle; Catholic doctrine doesn't require it.

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: "Alpha and Omega" echoes Isaiah's "first and last" and is shared by God and Jesus.

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: Jezebel is a nickname for a prophetess in Thyatira; the Laodicea "lukewarm" image reflects the local water supply.

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: The four horsemen (third is famine; oil and wine spared as class contrast, not Eucharist).

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: Seven means completeness, four means earth, 3.5 means limited evil.

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: Two witnesses (11), woman clothed with the sun (12; the church/Israel, not primarily Mary), beast "given" authority (13), the 144,000 (14), the closest NT image of hell (14:9-11).

notes.heading: Revelation
notes.note: Satan is bound and then must be released (20); death ends in the new creation (21:4).

notes.heading: Other topics
notes.note: **Arianism and "Aryan"** are unrelated; the similarity is spelling only.

notes.heading: Other topics
notes.note: **Last Supper**: Leonardo painted Renaissance Italian food, not a Passover seder.

notes.heading: Other topics
notes.note: **"Turn! Turn! Turn!"**, **Tolkien's debt to Maccabees** and **iconoclasm** came up as cultural spin-offs.

notes.heading: Other topics
notes.note: **70 CE** is the destruction of the Second Temple that reshaped both Judaism and Christianity.

open_questions: Gospel of Luke and John, read in full: how much of the "Jews" trajectory is present?
Pauline letters not yet discussed: Philippians, Thessalonians, Philemon.
Any further Apocrypha (Judith, Wisdom of Solomon) not yet covered.
Does any text address the "setup" problem directly, beyond Job?

points.heading: James
points.note: As we discussed earlier, interesting to see so many references to Jesus siblings (in this case the letter of James preface). Even if the authorship is disputed, I find it interesting that the existence of a brother named James is stated so matter-of-factly. How does the Catholic Church regard this? (James 1:1; Galatians 1:19; Mark 6:3)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: James
points.note: Why is friendship with the world seen as bad? (James 4:4-6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 1 Peter
points.note: Yet one more contradiction… doesn't the bible elsewhere state that Judas and all those that mistreated and crucified Jesus would be punished agree death? (1 Peter 2:23-25)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 1 Peter
points.note: Even that is not a complete recount, as the bible states that Jesus himself will be the judge after he comes back, so the judgement and reprisal is carried out by himself
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 1 Peter
points.note: I conceded the point. John 5:22 and Matthew 25:31-46 make Jesus the judge.
points.speaker: claude

points.heading: 1 Peter
points.note: Interesting to read this and see the ostentation of churches and clerics of different stripes (1 Peter 5:5; James 4:6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 2 Peter
points.note: It seems to me that while this is written supposedly by Peter, the real author wanted to address the tardiness of the second coming that had not happened at the real time it was written, around 125 CE. Is this how scholars think about it? (2 Peter 3:8-10)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 2 Peter
points.note: Yes, that's the mainstream view. Scholarly dates range from about 90 to 150 CE.
points.speaker: claude

points.heading: 1 John
points.note: Aren't these two portions of John contradictory? (1 John 1:8-10; 1 John 3:6-7)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 1 John
points.note: Circular logic… (1 John 4:5-6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: 1 John
points.note: Is there any discussion prior to this point about mortal vs non mortal sin? (1 John 5:16-17)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Where does the expression "the whore of Babylon" comes from?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: You asked this while reading the Apocrypha. The phrase comes from Revelation 17:1-5.
points.speaker: claude

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: What does the Catholic Church say about the author of the Apocalypse? (Revelation 1:4, 1:9, 21:14)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: This is the first time this expression is used, right? (Revelation 1:8)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: As a phrase, yes. The idea echoes Isaiah 44:6 ("I am the first and I am the last").
points.speaker: claude

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Is this supposed to be John talking to god? (Revelation 2:20-21)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: And who is he giving the authority to? (Revelation 2:26-29)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: What is the meaning of cold or hot here? (Revelation 3:15-16)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Here again, the you, is Jesus? (Revelation 5:9-10)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: So here the riders are introduced, what is the third? (Revelation 6:5-6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Why are oil and wine spared? (Revelation 6:6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Regarding 4, wouldn't wheel also be exempt as it is key for bread - the body of Christ?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: "Wheel" means wheat. Option 4 was the sacramental reading, and your objection counts against it.
points.speaker: claude

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: What's with the repeated use of the number seven, and to a lesser extent the number four in Revelations?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Who are the THEY in this portion? (Revelation 11:6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Is this Mary? (Revelation 12:6)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Where does the idea / festivity of Ascension show up in the bible?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Why is god allowing this? (Revelation 13:5)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: The problem of god setting up humans is everywhere, from genesis to revelations. There is no bible without it
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: But even where a choice is assumed, it is contrived and almost a set-up. God may not directly tempt them, but he creates the conditions that lead to the temptation
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: This is a sudden turn. Where does this come from? (Revelation 14:3-4)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Is this used by the Catholic church to justify celibacy? (Revelation 14:4)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: This is by my count the closest description of a Dantean hell. (Revelation 14:9-11)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Who places these constraints on god? (Revelation 20:1-3)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Revelation
points.note: Aren't people at this point immortal? (Revelation 21:3-4)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: Are the historical books part of the old or the new testament?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: To clarify, my assumption is that most aspects of the bible have little to no relation with facts, so the spirit of my questions are focused in clarifying my interpretation and ultimately to understand how believers and those who study it deal with those questions
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: What's the right way to pronounce the numbered books - e.g., 1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: What are the Apocryphal/Deuterocanonical Books of the Old Testament?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: Where does the practice and focus on circumcision comes from? I don't recall reading any explanation so far of why it is important, so my take away is that it is just a way to tell between groups. Is this right? (Genesis 17:9-14)
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: What is the year 70 ce.?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: What does CE stand for?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: General (not tied to one book)
points.note: Is Arianism at all related to the term as used by Nazis?
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Overall final observations
points.note: 1. The Bible is like a Rorshach test, where people can find justification for almost anything they already believe
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Overall final observations
points.note: 2. There is no coherent narrative or even ethics. Even the commandments are maleable - eg thou shall not kill, yet god and "his people" kills thousands.
points.speaker: me

points.heading: Overall final observations
points.note: The Hebrew verb (*ratsach*) usually means unlawful killing, so war and execution fall outside it. The stronger form of your point is about who counts as protected.
points.speaker: claude

points.heading: Overall final observations
points.note: 3. Playing on #2, the bible is a series of books written across more than a thousand years, and each individual book has an agenda for the time and place.
points.speaker: me
